definition: A spiritual teacher who establishes a religious doctrine or school of philosophy. The later acharyas , starting with Shankaracharya, established schools of philosophy by writing commentaries on the Prasthantrayi – the Brahmautras, Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita.
Opposite of dharma. That which transgresses dharma. Unrighteousness. Immorality.
The physical world. One’s body and everything in the material world around us made from the five elements (earth, water, fire, air, space).
The cosmic forces or deities that control nature and one’s senses. More commonly spelt as ‘adhidaiv’.
The inner self. Includes the mind, thoughts, feelings, and senses. It is the jiva’s connection to its own body and inner world.

Non-dual. The monotheistic doctrine propounded prominently by Shankaracharya that states that the ultimate reality is only one (i.e. non- dual) principal substance – nirgun Brahma – and that all else is merely an illusion.

1) I-ness-maker. One of the four aspects of the antahkaran , characterized by its function of giving rise to the sense of self, i.e. sense of individual existence. 2) On a cosmic level, a product of mahattattva , which is of three types – sattvik-ahamkar , rajas-ahamkar and tamas-ahamkar – and from which, in turn, the remaining elements are produced. By nature, it is passive, dense and totally ignorant.
A pastoral community traditionally engaged in agriculture and cattle- rearing.
Extraordinary divine power of God whereby he exercises restraint in his power to eclipse the infinite muktas of Akshardham by his own divine light and prevail alone.

1) Space/ether or vacuum. One of the five gross elements, from which the sthul body of Virat-Purush, i.e. the physical world, is formed. By nature, it provides space for all jivas , is the cause of the internal and external activities of their bodies, and is also where the prans , indriyas and antahkarans reside. The strongest of the five elements since it supports and pervades all the other four – yet remains wholly unaffected by them.

1) Imperishable. Second-highest of the five eternal realities; i.e. transcends everything except Purushottam. Also referred to as Aksharbrahma or Brahma. 2) In his personal form, Akshar serves Purushottam in his abode, Akshardham, and manifests as his ideal devotee, the Satpurush, on earth. Both forms are human in appearance. 3) In his impersonal form, Akshar is the abode of Purushottam, called Akshardham. 4) In his all-pervading anvay form, Akshar is called Chidakash.
See: Akshar.

The highest abode. The divine abode of Parabrahma Purushottam Bhagwan Swaminarayan, where he is forever seated before countless muktas , who have attained qualities similar to those of Akshar. The impersonal form of Akshar.
A jiva that has attained ultimate liberation and resides forever in Akshardham with a divine body.
Also called Maha-Purush, Mul-Purush, or simply, Purush.

1) Form of Akshar. One who has qualities similar to those of Akshar. Used to describe the spiritual state of akshar-muktas . Highest level of faith or spiritual status is to become aksharrup and worship Purushottam. 2) Is also sometimes used to describe things that have attained qualities similar to Akshar through his contact, e.g., light.
Knowledge of the eyes. A type of brahmavidya by which one sees one’s atma and the form of God within the eyes.
Region beyond this realm.
No-moon day signifying the last day of a lunar month, i.e. the 15th day of the dark half of an Indian calendar month. New moon.
Without death. Refers to the divine nectar churned from the ocean by the devas and the demons, known to grant immortality to those who drink it.
Bird of fire. Large, legendary bird that never lands on the ground and has the strength to carry seven elephants.
Born from an egg. Category of life forms born from eggs, such as birds, reptiles, and others.
A traditional Indian upper garment with long sleeves, worn by men, often tied at the chest, reaching down to the knees.

Inner faculty. The complete mind which comprises of four aspects, each characterized by its individual functions: called the man when generating thoughts and desires; the buddhi when consolidating thoughts, making decisions and resolutions, forming convictions, or discriminating; the chitt when repeatedly contemplating or focusing; and the ahamkar when forming a sense of being. Normally used in the singular since all four are aspects of the one antahkaran , but also often referred to as being four different antahkarans .
Inner controller. Power of God to reside within a jiva , ishwar , and others, and control their every action. Also implies God’s ability to know their innermost thoughts and feelings.
Fundamental, universal and atom-like unit of matter. Monad. Smallest building block of existence.
Not separate. Associated. Connected. When used for God, implies immanent, i.e. inherently existing within.

Extraordinary divine power of God whereby he can eclipse even Akshar – in the form of Akshardham – and uphold the infinite muktas by himself, implying that he is the supporter of all, but that he himself is totally independent.
Path of light that a spiritually enlightened soul takes after death to reach God’s abode.
One of the four purusharths , allowing for the fulfilment of desires for material objects, in particular wealth.
Hindu ritual of waving lighted wicks before the murti of God as an act of worship.
1) Third of the eight steps of Ashtanga Yoga, entailing physical exercises of postures for soundness of body, which promotes concentration. 2) Seat or mat one sits on.
1) Opposite of sat . Transient, i.e. perishable, changing and bound by the constraints of time. 2) False. Not true.
1) Opposite of satya . Transient, i.e. perishable and changing, and bound by the constraints of Time. 2) False. Not true. 3) Imaginary or illusory according to the Advaita doctrine.
First month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, normally beginning between June and July.

Eightfold path of yoga comprising eight progressive steps leading ultimately to yoga, i.e. union with God. The eight steps are: yam (restraint), niyam (personal observance), asan (physical posture), pranayam (breath control), pratyahar (withdrawal of the senses), dharna (concentration), dhyan (meditation), and samadhi (trance).
Fourth month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, normally beginning between September and October.
Type of tree whose leaves are used in rituals and on auspicious occasions as decoration.

1) One who believes in the existence of God, or more generally, one who is religiously-inclined. 2) Also refers to people or shastras that accept the authority and authenticity of the Vedas. 3) One who accepts the moral law of karma.
Form of envy, in which faults are attributed to the virtues of the person of whom one is jealous.
First realm beneath Mrutyulok, where demons reside. Seventh realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .

1) The jiva or soul, distinct from the physical, subtle and causal bodies. 2) Generally, that which pervades, inspires and governs. Thus, also refers to God as the pervader, inspirer and governor of the physical and non-physical world, i.e. shariri .

One who offers atmanivedanam , the ninth type of bhakti, i.e. a devotee who has totally surrendered themselves to God. One whose every action is an offering to God and who has God at the centre of their every action.

1) Final dissolution. Destruction of all the countless millions of brahmands , when even Prakruti-Purush – the cause of countless Pradhan-Purushes – draws in countless brahmands within itself, and is then eclipsed by the light of Aksharbrahma. In atyantik-pralay , only Purushottam, Akshar, and the akshar- muktas remain. 2) On the individual level, also called jnan-pralay . See: jnan-pralay.
Type of small shrub whose leaves have inherent healing properties.
Synonymous with maya . False understanding of the nature of reality. Ignorance.

Of the three bodies of Virat-Purush and other ishwars , the causal body. Analogous to the karan body of the jivas . The body from which an ishwar’s virat (gross) body and sutratma (subtle) body evolve, and is thus also considered as the maya of ishwar .

Resident of Ayodhya. Ayodhya, the birthplace of Bhagwan Ram, is a city in northern India where Bhagwan Swaminarayan’s family lived for several years after moving from Chhapaiya, Bhagwan Swaminarayan’s birthplace. In the context of the , the term refers to Bhagwan Swaminarayan’s family.
Mental state of apprehension at the possibility of becoming attached again to objects recognized as false and to which the ties of affection have been severed.
Sacred hermitage known for badri-trees; regarded as the celestial abode of Nar- Narayan, where liberated souls perform austerities to please God and attain liberation through human birth.
Third month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, typically beginning between August and September.
Divinely ordained dharma focused on devotion to God; this form of dharma is not different from bhakti itself; also called ekantik dharma.

Hindu shastra that forms a portion of the epic Mahabharat (Bhishma-parva, chapters 25–42), in which Bhagwan Krishna enlightens Arjun on karma, bhakti and jnan , and inspires him to selflessly fulfil his duty of fighting for dharma against adharma by the strength and will of God.
Ideal devotee of God, referring to the Satpurush.
Community traditionally employed as court poets or bards, known for composing praise poetry for royalty; also called Barot.

Ancient India, considered to have stretched from present-day Turkey to present-day Burma, and beyond the Himalayan mountain range. Regarded as the best of the nine regions of Jambu-dwip because of the presence of God’s avatars or saints who enable liberation.
Earthly realm. Mrutyulok.
One of the five gross elements – earth, water, fire, air, space – forming the physical universe. Collectively called the five bhuts or five mahabhuts .
First realm above Mrutyulok, where lesser devas reside. Ninth realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .
Cloth wrapped to cover head, ears, and cheeks for warmth during cold weather.
Tree with thorns, delicate flowers, and small sour fruits (bors ); grows in the wild due to resilient roots.
Tree known for extremely fragrant, delicate, white flowers.

1) Second-highest of the five eternal realities, i.e. transcends everything except Parabrahma. Also called Akshar, or Aksharbrahma. 2) Often taken to refer to the Brahma of the shushka -Vedantis, i.e. the nirgun , formless and non-dual ultimate reality, apart from which, they claim, all else is merely an illusion.

The ishwar responsible for the creation of the brahmand and the life forms within it. Part of the trinity of ishwars , along with Vishnu (the sustainer) and Shiv (the destroyer), responsible for the governance of one brahmand . Not to be confused with Brahma, the second-highest of the five eternal realities.
1) One who observes brahmacharya , i.e. leads a life of celibacy. 2) One who is in the first stage of life in the traditional Hindu four stages of life, i.e. brahmacharya stage.

1) Celibacy and self-restraint. Renunciates observe eight-fold brahmacharya – abstinence from associating with the opposite gender in the following ways: (1) shravanam – listening to or of (2) keertanam – talking to or of (3) keli – frolicking with (4) prekshanam – intentionally looking at 5) guhyabhashanam – privately conversing with (6) sankalpa – fantasizing about (7) adhyavasaya – thinking of (8) kriya – intercourse with. For householders men and women, brahmacharya constitutes marital fidelity.
First of the four stages of life, dedicated to study and celibacy.
Supreme abode of God, also called Akshardham.
A day of Brahmā, equal to 4,320,000,000 human years; period between creation and destruction of the world.
1) Realm of God. Akshardham. 2) Realm of Brahmā. Highest realm in the 14- realm system of a brahmand . Also called Satyalok.
1) Palace of God. Abode of God. Akshardham. 2) Formless and pure chaitanya form of Akshar. Also called Chidakash.

Individual universe comprising 14 realms. Each brahmand , created and sustained by a Pradhan-Purush pair, contains a trinity of Brahmā, Vishnu, and Shiv as the governing devas. The 14 realms of each brahmand are, in descending order: Satyalok, Taplok, Janlok, Maharlok, Swarglok, Bhuvarlok, Mrutyulok, Atal, Vital, Sutal, Talatal, Mahatal, Rasatal, Patal. See also: Glossary entry on each realm.
1) Abode of God. Akshardham. 2) Also refers to Brahmalok, as realm of Brahmā.
Mystical opening in the crown of the head – at the end of the sushumna nadi – through which the jiva leaves the body on death or during samadhi and reaches higher realms.
A sage of the highest order, surpassing a rajarshi , and known for austere spirituality.
Form of Brahma. Possessing virtues similar to those of Brahma. Same as aksharrup .
1) Formless aspect of Brahma, i.e. Chidakash. 2) Also refers to atma , which is characterized by eternal existence.
State of divine, deep-sleep-like consciousness; the all-pervading formless aspect of Brahma (Chidakash).
Form or embodiment of Brahma.

Knowledge of Brahma, i.e. God. Knowledge that guides one on the path to God- realization. Bruhadaranya Upanishad Also called ‘Bruhadaranyaka’. One of the most important of the principal Upanishads, belonging to the Yajur Veda, and ascribed to Yagnavalkya Rishi. Teachings centre around modes of worship, contemplation and identity with Brahma.
Traditional type of cloth from central India.
Intellect; faculty for decision-making, discernment, and forming convictions; one of the four aspects of the inner mind (antahkaran).
Consciousness. The essence of the atma . A higher awareness transcending the physical.
Living or animate things that possess consciousness (chaitanya).
Tenth month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, typically between March and April.
Wooden, strapless sandals worn by renunciates for simplicity and personal discipline.
Centres of spiritual energy (‘wheels’) within the subtle body, regarded in yoga to be seats of consciousness.
Fragrant, delicate, and typically white jasmine flower, often blooming in the month of Shravan.
Type of flower, usually yellow in colour.
A type of gram, similar to dried chickpeas.
Small, round mark – usually either of kumkum or of sandalwood paste – applied in the centre of the forehead indicating one’s Hindu affiliation.

A strict fasting regimen where food intake is regulated according to the waxing and waning of the moon. For example, one form is to increase food intake from one morsel of food at the beginning of a new lunar month rising to 15 morsels on Punam, then decreasing again to a complete fast by Amas; or, beginning with 15 morsels of food at the beginning of a new month and decreasing to a complete fast on Punam, then increasing again to 15 by Amas. Other forms involve having only eight morsels a day, or four morsels twice a day, or merely three morsels a day.
Celestial minstrel or a class of people traditionally employed to compose and recite verses of praise.
Possessing consciousness (chaitanya); animate.
A principal Upanishad of the Sam Veda, focusing on the significance of AUM, the atma , contemplation, and life after death.
Type of rich, embroidered cloth.
Crest-like tuft of cloth either emerging from the end of a pagh or left hanging from one side. Sometimes inserted into a pagh when made of a string of flowers.

The formless, pure, all-supporting and all- pervading conscious form of Akshar. It is extremely luminous, not subject to change and eternal. Distinct from the gross element akash, which evolves from tamogun and which undergoes creation and destruction. Also known as Brahma.
Divine gemstone that fulfils all the wishes of its possessor.
Mind/consciousness. One of the four aspects of the antahkaran, responsible for contemplating, focusing, and storing mental impressions
Sewn upper garment for males, pleated at the chest and shorter than an angarkhu .
Knowledge that explains how God lives inside even the small space of the heart – called dahar-akash . Knowledge of Chidakash.
A royal or feudal court of residence, typically with a central courtyard.

The six classical systems of Hindu philosophy that offer distinct perspectives on the world, soul, and God: Nyaya – Logic and epistemology; Vaisheshika – Atomism and metaphysics; Sankhya – Dualism of consciousness and matter; Yoga – Practical methods for self-realization and union with God; Purva Mimansa – Emphasis on Vedic rituals and duties; Uttar Mimansa (Vedanta) – Philosophical teachings of the Upanishads, particularly on the nature of the atma , the world, reality and personal experience. Among its sub-schools are Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita, and Akshar-Purushottam Darshan
Realm of the devas; also known as Swarglok.
1) Bhagwan Swaminarayan himself. 2) Family of Dharmadev [Bhagwan Swaminarayan’s father]. Refers to Bhagwan Swaminarayan’s family.
Shastras outlining the laws and principles of civil and social conduct, integrating spirituality and daily duties; part of Smruti literature literature.
Concentration. Sixth of the eight steps of Ashtanga Yoga, entailing focusing the mind.
The North Star (Polaris), used for navigation due to its fixed position.
Continuous chanting of God’s name, often with musical accompaniment; also pronounced dhun .
Unstitched lower garment for males, wrapped around the waist and legs; also known as dhoti.
Meditation. Seventh of the eight steps of Ashtanga Yoga, involving sustaining a clear and calm concentrated state.

Last day of the Vikram Samvat Indian year, i.e. day of Amas of the month of Aso. Very holy and joyous Hindu festival celebrating the return of Ram Bhagwan to Ayodhya from his 14-year exile, and the victory of good over evil – signified by the lighting of lamps.
Cheap, inferior quality of spinach generally eaten only by the extremely poor.
A jasmine variety with white flowers, noted for its beauty when swaying in the wind – from which it gets its name.
The seer or observer; typically referring to the atma , but can also denote God as the inner observer within each atma .
Visible; an object of perception, often referring to the physical body or the entire visible world.
Rich delicacy made of sweetened milk and rice, garnished with aromatic spices and nuts.
Pair of small kettle drums, similar to tabla, used for rhythm in folk and devotional music. Also spelt as dukkad.
Dualistic philosophical doctrine asserting the eternal distinction between the jiva (soul) and God, contrasting with Advaita which propounds their non- duality.
Third of the four cosmic ages (yugas ), lasting 864,000 human years, characterized by a decline in purity and righteousness.
Island or continent-like landmass.

1) 11th day of both bright and dark halves of a lunar month, traditionally observed with fasting and special religious observance. 2) Also refers to the divine woman created from the light of God’s ten indriyas and mind, who defeated the demon Mur Danav.

A former sadhu, who has left the monastic order due to personal misconduct or inability to conform to the renunciate regimen – and now travels alone, which is against Swaminarayan monastic rules requiring sadhus to travel at least in pairs.

A person of elevated spiritual state who offers devotion (bhakti ) to God coupled with dharma (righteousness), jnan (spiritual knowledge), and vairagya (detachment) – the four virtues of ekantik dharma.
A devotee of the highest order who perfectly embodies dharma, jnan, vairagya, and bhakti, has no desires apart from God, and worships God while realizing oneself as brahmarup.
Bhakti combined with dharma, jnan and vairagya . Synonymous with ekantik dharma.

Collective term for the four virtues of dharma (religious disciplines and duties), jnan (spiritual knowledge), vairagya (detachment from worldly pleasures), and bhakti (devotion) coupled with the knowledge of God’s glory – the cultivating of which leads one to become an ekantik bhakta who crosses God’s maya and attains his abode. Also called bhagvat dharma.
Highest level of sadhu, one who has attained the ekantik state.
Refers to the ideal ekantik sadhu, the Satpurush.
Ninth month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, generally beginning between February and March.
Long piece of cloth twisted and tied around the head as a headdress.
Celestial being renowned for expertise in music, song and dance in the celestial realms.
Fiery eagle-like bird with white head and red wings, and a golden male body. Serves as Lord Vishnu’s vehicle.
Traditional Indian measure of distance equivalent to about 1.5 to 1.75 miles.
Duration of time equalling approximately 24 minutes in traditional Indian timekeeping.
Short form for Bhagavad Gita, a foundational Hindu shastra.
Celestial abode of Shri Krishna described in the Purans as supremely beautiful.
Protectors of cows. Cowherds of Vrundavan present during the time of Bhagwan Krishna. Male devotees exemplifying love and bhakti for God.
Protectors of cows. Wives of the cowherds of Vrundavan during the time of Bhagwan Krishna. Exemplifying ideal bhakti towards God.
Yogic posture where heels are tucked into the groin, toes folded under buttocks, and large toes held from behind the back; aids brahmacharya ; also called gorakshasan or bhadrasan.
Flower of the chrysanthemum genus, noted for blooming out of season; varieties include red and yellow with small pointed petals; also called sevanti .

Quality. Principle quality of Prakruti, or maya . There are three in total: sattvagun (goodness, i.e. awareness), rajogun (passion, i.e. desires) and tamogun (darkness, i.e. unawareness, lethargy). All beings are affected by the influence of one or a combination of these three gunas of maya until they become gunatit . With respect to the influence of the gunas on jivas and ishwars , the gunas elicit in people’s minds three different types of moods as follows: a person in sattvagun is calm, placid, peaceful; a person in rajogun is desirous, active, sensual; a person in tamogun is volatile, lethargic, drowsy.
One who transcends all three gunas of maya (sattva, rajas, tamas ), and is free from the influence of maya.
Portion of Bhagwan Krishna’s final teachings (Shrimad Bhagvat, canto XI, chapter 25) to his friend and statesman, Uddhav, regarding the classification and characteristics of the three gunas .
Large yellowish-orange flower; commonly known as marigold.
Gujarati shastra of the Swaminarayan Fellowship poetically detailing the life and work of Bhagwan Swaminarayan.
Supplement to the Mahabharat, detailing Vishnu’s lineage and Bhagwan Krishna’s life in over 16,000 verses.
Small tree with white flowers, commonly found in the Kutch region of Gujarat.
Spiritual space within the heart, regarded as the seat of the inner self.
One of the three major energy channels (nadis ) described in yogic traditions. It runs along the left side of the spine and controls the mind, emotions, and inner awareness.
Realm of Indra, the god of rain and king of the devas. Also known as Swarglok.

Senses or faculties. They are the sensory and motor faculties through which an individual perceives and interacts with the world, both externally and internally. They are traditionally classified into two main groups: jnan- indriyas (cognitive senses), the five senses for receiving information from the external world – eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin; and karma-indriyas (conative senses), the five faculties for performing actions and expressing oneself – hands, feet, speech, genitals, and anus. A third component, the man (mind), is considered the eleventh indriya . It serves as the coordinator, processing inputs from the jnan-indriyas and directing the activity of the karma-indriyas .
One’s chosen or beloved deity. The form of God that a person feels the closest to, loves the most, and worships with full faith.

Second of the five eternal realities. Infinite in number. Similar to jiva with respect to being bound by maya – i.e. composed of the 24 elementsb, having three bodies, three states, three gunas , desires, and other features – but involved in the processes and lordship of the brahmands , and thus endowed by God with greater powers. Brahmā, Vishnu, Shiv and all realities greater than them upwards to Prakruti- Purush, are considered ishwars .

History. The two Indian historical epics – Ramayan and Mahabharat – that are among the most popular and widely accepted of all Hindu shastras. Both are interwoven with stories and sub-stories incorporating social ideals as well as philosophical and spiritual principles. Considered a part of the Smruti literature.
Non-living, inanimate. Opposite of chaitanya . That which is without consciousness.

Inanimate (non-chaitanya) constituents of the world – either as eight elements: pruthvi , jal , tej , vayu , akash , mahattattva , Pradhan-Prakruti and Mul-Prakruti; or, per Bhagavad Gita: pruthvi , jal , tej , vayu , akash , man , buddhi and ahamkar .
Traditional Hindu greeting or farewell.
Traditional greeting or farewell among Swaminarayan devotees; used by Shriji Maharaj in the .
Of or relating to Jainism, the non-Vedic Indian religion of non-violence and strict asceticism; a follower of Jainism.
Fourth realm above Mrutyulok, where Bhrugu and other rishis reside. The 12th realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .
Birthday of Bhagwan Krishna (Shravan vadi 8), celebrated by Vaishnavs with devotional festivals.
Water. One of the five gross elements. By nature, it binds substances, softens, moistens, sustains life, quenches thirst, subdues heat and is abundant.
Yogic cleansing practice using water to clean the lower intestines, promoting physical and mental clarity.
Category of beings born from a womb; includes mammals and humans.
Pair of small, traditional cymbals – slightly larger than manjiras – used in the accompaniment of other percussion instruments.

Individual living soul, bound by maya, experiencing repeated births and deaths; possesses three bodies (gross, subtle, causal) and three states (waking, dream, deep sleep); first of the five eternal realities.
Individual soul; jiva .
1) Spiritual knowledge leading to enlightenment. In particular, the knowledge of one’s atma and the form and glory of Paramatma. 2) Also means atma - realization.

Cognitive senses. Sense organs. The five faculties by which the jiva receives knowledge of the external world: eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin. Each jnan- indriya includes both the gross physical organ (e.g., the eye) and its corresponding subtle cognitive power (e.g., the sense of sight). Thus, jnan- indriyas represent the complete system of sensory perception – the physical tools and the inner capacity to perceive.
State in which all mayik influences dissolve for the individual through spiritual knowledge (jnan ); one perceives only pure chaitanya and God’s form (akin to atyantik- pralay for that person).
The 12th month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, starting between May and June.
Celestial abode of Bhagwan Shiv.

Time; the continuous flow enabling the succession of events (past, present, future), often equated with destruction and death, and regarded as one of God’s powers from which the soul is liberated upon attaining moksha .
The fourth and current age (yug ) in Hindu cosmology; known as the Age of Darkness, lasting 432,000 years, it is marked by a decline in virtue and spiritual values.

Tree that lasts for a kalp . Special tree possessing the magical power to fulfil the wishes of anyone who sits under it. One of the 14 divine objects that emerged from the churning of the oceans by the devas and demons.
One of the four purusharths , allowing for the regulated fulfilment of one’s personal and social desires.
A community of the Vaishya varna traditionally engaged in farming and rearing cattle.

Double-threaded necklace, usually made of tulsi beads, received by satsangis upon initiation into the Satsang Fellowship, and worn as a sign of their affiliation to God. Derived from noun kantha , meaning neck.
Portion of the Shrimad Bhagvat (canto 3, chapters 25–33) consisting of Kapilji’s preachings to his mother, Devhuti.

Causal. Of the three bodies of the jiva , the causal body, i.e. the jiva’s desires or maya – which causes the jiva to take birth again. By nature, it itself is ignorance, which has been fused with the jiva since time immemorial. It retains the jiva’s sanchit karmas and is the cause of the sthul and sukshma bodies just as a seed is the cause of a tree.

Conative senses. Organs of action. The five faculties through which the jiva performs actions in the external world: hands – for grasping or giving, feet – for movement, speech (mouth) – for speaking, genitals – for reproduction, and anus – for elimination Each karma-indriya consists of a gross physical organ and a subtle conative power – the inner force or will to act. Together, they form the jiva’s instruments of expression and interaction with the world.
A practitioner of karma yoga, achieving spiritual progress through selfless action without attachment to results; typically a householder pursuing liberation while fulfilling worldly duties.
Type of flower, usually red, white or yellow in colour.
Fifth month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, normally beginning between October and November.
Extraordinary divine power of God to eclipse the infinite muktas of Akshardham by his own divine light, and prevail alone.

Also called Katha Upanishad. One of the most important of the principal Upanishads, belonging to the Krishna Yajur Veda. Includes the enlightening story of how the young Nachiketa received the knowledge of immortality from Yam, the god of death.
A community of the Kshatriya varna traditionally strong and well-built. Type of Rajput. Native(s) of Kathiawad, a region in Gujarat.
A community of people historically associated with administrative, clerical, and scholarly professions.
Perfect or ultimate jnan . Specific philosophical term of the Jain school describing – as propounded in their nastik philosophy – the final state of realization.
Continent. Large land mass or region.
Cloth that may be worn as a dhotiyu or as an upper garment.
Rich item of food made of sweetened milk and rice, garnished with aromatic spices and nuts, and usually served hot.
Fine silken fabric brocaded with golden or silver threads.
One of the many Upanishads.

Inferior quality of grain that lacks in nutrition. Similar in size and shape to mustard seeds, but white in colour. Stored in times of famine because of its resilience against extreme weather conditions and time, but generally eaten only by the poor.
Specific community of people traditionally living as boat people, fishermen or farmers.

kriyaman karmas Deeds whose consequences are in the process of being formed. Current deeds – including words and even thoughts – which will eventually be added to the stock of karmas (sanchit karmas) until they ripen to be bear fruit as prarabdha karmas, either later in the present life or in a future life. kruchchhra chandrayan Form of stern austerity entailing regulating one’s intake of food over prolonged periods of time, generally performed as a form of atonement for a grave sin.
Literally ‘field’; in philosophy, denotes the body or material realm, over which the self (kshetragna ) is master; also means any defined territory or place.
The ‘knower of the field’; typically, the soul (atma ) that is aware of and presides over the body (kshetra ).
Ocean of milk. A divine ocean where Lord Vishnu rests upon Shesh, lord of the serpents.

Follower of an anti-Vedic cult that falsely propagates the five m’s as a means to liberation, namely: madya (alcohol), mans (meat), matsya (fish), mudra (tantric, i.e. occult markings) and maithun (illicit sex).

An austere yogic practice to help cleanse the inner parts of the body – which in turn helps in the observance of brahmacharya . The practice involves drinking a considerable amount of water, swirling it around the stomach, and then discharging it out again through the mouth.
A person who is bad company, i.e. a bad influence on one’s spiritual progress, and leads one astray from satsang.
Sweet item of food made principally of flour, ghee, and gur or sugar, shaped into small balls.
Period of time approximately equal to 150th of a second, traditionally noted as eight times the time taken to pierce a lotus- leaf with a needle, or one- sixtieth of the time taken to blink.

School of philosophy adhering to the doctrine of Madhvacharya, a 13th century South Indian Vaishnav acharya . He propounded a doctrine of pure dualism, wherein there is an essential and eternal distinction between God and all other beings and things.
Dialect specific to Magadh, the southern region of present-day Bihar. Language of the ancient Jain and Buddhist shastras.
Sixth month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, normally beginning between November and December.
Eighth month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, normally beginning between January and February.

Great epic of India. Popular Hindu shastra revolving around the family feud between the Pandavs and the Kauravs, culminating in the great battle, the Mahabharat war. One of the two Itihas shastras. With over 100,000 verses, it is the world’s longest poem.

Great elements. The mahabhuts are the five gross elements – pruthvi (earth), jal (water), tej (fire or energy), vayu (air), and akash (space or ether) – that constitute the physical universe. They evolve from tamas- ahamkar and are the building blocks of the cosmic form (Virat-Purush) and ishwars (cosmic deities). Each mahabhut arises from a subtler cause known as its tanmatra (subtle essence): pruthvi – originates from gandh (smell), jal – from ras (taste), tej – from rupa (form or sight), vayu – from sparsh (touch), and akash – from shabda (sound). Together, the mahabhuts form the gross, perceptible aspects of creation, while their tanmatras form the subtle sensory causes
Also called Mul-maya, Mul-Prakruti, or simply, Prakruti.
Technical term referring to one of the 11 efforts required to pronounce certain syllables requiring an extended breath.
Also called Mul-Purush, Akshar-Purush, or simply, Purush.
Third realm above Mrutyulok, where Aryama and other ancestral devas reside. The 11th realm from the bottom in the 14- realm system of a brahmand .
Fifth realm below Mrutyulok, where nocturnals reside. Third realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .

Cosmic intelligence or great principle. Mahattattva is the first principle to evolve from the union of Pradhan (primordial matter) and Purush (cosmic spirit). It is considered the cosmic counterpart of the jiva’s chitt (mind-stuff or memory faculty), and acts as the universal field of awareness and potential. By its nature, the entire jagat (universe) exists within mahattattva in a subtle, unmanifest form. It is described as unchanging (avikari ), luminous (self- revealing, full of knowledge), pure, pervaded by sattvagun , and passive – it does not act on its own but serves as the base for further evolutes (like ahamkar and tanmatras ).
Malhar. A specific raga of Indian music. Considered to induce rainfalls if sung correctly.
Mind. One of the four aspects of the antahkaran , characterized by its functions of generating thoughts and desires, and governing all the indriyas .
Thinking. Contemplation. Deep reflection.
Group. In the time of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, the sadhus were often formed into groups. Each group travelled and preached in different regions.
Pair of small, traditional cymbals.
The mind in the form of a wheel. The mind, seen as an incessantly turning wheel, whose ten spokes are taken to be the ten indriyas .
Nerve or channel wherein the mind resides, transmitting energy within the inner body of a person and allowing the flow of desires and thoughts.
Mental worship. Form of worship in which one devoutly performs puja, offers arti , thal , and other forms of devotion to God mentally.

Oldest and considered to be the most authoritative of the ancient Smruti shastras, serving even today as a sourcebook of Hindu culture and customs. Its 2,685 verses incorporate day-to-day laws and duties for people of every strata of society. Ascribed to the primordial King Manu, the father of mankind.
Of the 14 Manus that reign sequentially during one day of Brahmā, the duration of the reign of one Manu. Duration of time equalling 306,720,000 human years.
Follower of the Vam-marg (Cult of Lust), an anti-Vedic cult that propagates illicit sex and other Veda-prohibited practices.

Closely aligned with jealousy and envy. Signifies a feeling of resentment or displeasure at another person’s good fortune, success, or possessions – whether it be of a person of equal standing or otherwise.
a traditional unit of mass used in British India varying in value from 25 pounds (11 kg) to 160 pounds (72½ kg) depending on the geographical region.

The divine power of illusion and the fundamental substance of creation, governed by the three gunas ; causes the soul’s entanglement in worldly existence and must be transcended for liberation. Third of the five eternal realities.
Of, or pertaining to maya . Opposite of divine.
A small, well-ventilated room atop a traditional residential haveli structure. Sometimes, it also refers to the entire building itself.
Delicate flower of the jasmine genus, white in colour and extremely sweet in fragrance. Traditionally used in offerings to murtis of God.
Portion of the Mahabharat (Shanti-parva, chapters 174–365) comprising of Bhishma’s teachings from his bed of arrows to King Yudhishthir after the conclusion of the Mahabharat war.
Rich fabric with silky finish woven with golden or silver threads and detailed, decorative edges.
(Pronounced moth ). Very cheap and inferior type of moss-like spinach found to grow on riverbanks, eaten only by the extremely poor.
Type of double-sided drum. Traditional Indian percussion instrument played to supply rhythm in the singing of devotional songs.
Realm of death. Seventh realm in the 14- realm system of a brahmand , where everyone and everything is subject to death; the only realm where human birth and ultimate liberation is possible.

A liberated soul. A resident of any abode of God who has been freed from a lower plane of existence to a more spiritually elevated state. There are varying levels of spiritual elevation, i.e. muktas of Badrikashram, Shvetdwip, Golok, and so on. The highest level of mukta , akshar-mukta , has attained ultimate liberation and is free from the bondage of maya and the consequent cycle of births and deaths.
Also called mahamaya , Mul-maya, or simply, Prakruti.
Prakruti-Purush.
Also called Maha-Purush, Akshar-Purush, or simply, Purush.
sage, ascetic.
Sacred image of God used to offer worship.

Conduit. Nerve or channel transmitting energy within the inner bodies of a person and interconnecting the chakras . There are said to be 72,000 nadis in all, of which three are major: ida nadi , pingala nadi , and sushumna nadi .
Revised edition of the Panchratra Tantra composed by Naradji.

Realm to which damned sinners are consigned and compelled to suffer at the hands of Yam, the god of death, and his servants. Often used in the plural to signify the various infernal regions. After serving an appropriate amount of time, based on the extent of the sins, the jiva eventually returns to the cycle of births and deaths.

1) Non-believer. Opposite of astik . Person who does not believe in the existence of God, or more generally, one who is not religiously inclined. 2) Can also describe people or shastras that do not accept the authority and authenticity of the Vedas. 3) One who proclaims as false the moral dos and don’ts prescribed by the shastras.
Deep, sustained meditation and contemplation, especially in Vedanta, on the teachings heard and understood from a guru.
Blink. Duration of time equal to approximately two-fifths of a second, traditionally taken to be the time taken to blink.

1) Stimulated dissolution. Destruction of the lower 10 realms of the 14- realm system of a brahmand including swarg , Mrutyulok and patal . This is stimulated by the end of the 14-manvantar day of Virat- Purush, i.e. when his equally long night falls. 2) Brahmā’s deep sleep state – when all adjuncts of ishwar are absorbed – which lasts as long as his day, equivalent to 4,320,000,000 human years.
Refers to a liberated soul of Shvetdwip, who performs intense austerities and is said to survive there without any food.

1) Without gunas . Not possessing any attributes of the three gunas – sattvagun , rajogun and tamogun – i.e. transcends all mayik qualities. Divine. 2) In some philosophical contexts, also used to mean ‘without form or qualities,’ as applied to the supreme being.
Without alternatives or doubts. Adjective describing faith or state of being in which one sees only God – but no doubts or distinctions remain whatsoever, i.e. a state of perfect realization.

1) Highest state of realization, in which one sees only God – but no doubts or distinctions remain whatsoever, i.e. a state of perfect realization. 2) The eighth and final stage – and ultimate goal – of Ashtanga Yoga.
Adjective describing that which is without any adjuncts. This describes maya in her causal state when she is devoid of all the things that may develop from her, i.e. pruthvi , jal , tej , and others.
A 100-verse poetical shastra expounding ethical values and morals. Composed by Bhartruhari, the famous fifth-century king- turned-sannyasi.
1) Constant dissolution. The day-to-day dying of countless individual devas, demons, humans and others. 2) The jivas state of deep sleep – when all adjuncts of the jiva are absorbed.

The path of turning away from worldly pursuits and desires, and directing one’s focus inward towards God and the Self. It is the spiritual path of detachment, renunciation, and inner contemplation. Even householders can follow a nivrutti mindset by living in the world but remaining detached from it – serving God while maintaining inner renunciation.
Dharma characterized by nivrutti . Path of renunciation or path of inactivity from worldly pursuits.

1) Moral and spiritual disciplines, and religious codes of conduct prescribed by God, the Satpurush, or the shastras to protect a devotee on the path to God. Niyams may relate to either the observance of dharma or the observance of bhakti. Observance of niyams keeps the devotee fit to travel closer to God and ultimately earns the grace of God. Transgressing niyams causes the devotee to fall from the path of God. Bhagwan Swaminarayan has outlined the basic niyams for all his followers in the Shikshapatri. 2) Second step of Ashtanga Yoga, entailing observance of religious practices and the codes of dharma for the control and refinement of the mind.
One of the 18 major Purans, with about 55,000 verses describing cosmology, creation, and pilgrimage rites.
A period equivalent to one day of Brahmā (4.32 billion years), during which the process of creation – including the embodiment of Marichi and other beings – takes place.
Long, thin piece of cloth tied around the head like a turban to form a traditional headdress.
Type of mrudang or double-sided drum. Traditional Indian percussion instrument with a deep, mellow sound, played to supply rhythm when singing devotional songs.
Duration of time equal to approximately 24 seconds.
A Vaishnav shastra composed by Vasudev Bhagwan, authoritative for rituals, worship, and temple construction. Revered highly by Vaishnavs, traditionally part of the Agamas.

The objects of the five senses. These are the external phenomena that the five sense organs (jnan-indriyas ) perceive: rup – sights (seen by the eyes), shabda – sounds (heard by the ears), gandha – smells (detected by the nose), ras – tastes (experienced by the tongue), sparsh – touches (felt by the skin). Though each category includes a vast range of specific experiences, together they form the panchvishays – the sensory inputs through which the jiva engages with the world. In spiritual practice, attachment to these objects is considered a key source of bondage, and detachment from them is essential for inner purification.
The Supreme Absolute Reality, God; highest of the five eternal realities, transcending Brahma. Also called Paramatma or Purushottam.
The Supreme Soul; refers to the highest of the five eternal realities – God, who is immanent in all beings. Also called Parabrahma or Purushottam.
Ideal devotee of God, referring to the Satpurush.
Ideal sadhu of God, referring to the Satpurush.
Ideal ekantik sadhu of God, referring to the Satpurush.

Supreme swan. A male sadhu of the highest order, characterized by his ability to discriminate between sat and asat – just as swans were traditionally considered to be able to distinguish between milk mixed with water. Traditionally, they renounce not only worldly pursuits, but also all religious accessories such as rites, symbols and objects – daily worship, chandlo , kanthi , and others – and lead a life of travelling and preaching. In the time of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, there was an illustrious band of 2,000 learned, talented and saintly sadhus of which 500 were initiated into the paramhansa order. These were later re-initiated as sadhus and returned to performing all traditional religious rites and rituals, but were still known as paramhansas .
Duration of time equal to 1 x 1017 human years; half a kalp, or half the lifespan of Brahmā.
One of the principal ancient Smruti shastras. Ascribed to Parashar Rishi, father of Vyas.
Philosopher’s stone. Magical gem that turns iron into gold.

Male renunciate in the time of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, similar to a sadhu, but one whose niyams were not as stringent. They observed brahmacharya in general but were allowed to talk with women, were allowed to touch money but not keep it for themselves. Most parshads shaved their heads like other sadhus, but wore a white – not saffron – dhotiyu and upper garment.
Collective term for the region of realms below Mrutyulok.

Nerve or channel of a masculine nature transmitting intellectual and mental energy within the inner body of a person, where the current of energy flows upward and ends on the right side of the body. One of the three major nadis .
Seventh month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, normally beginning between December and January.
The unmanifest, primordial form of matter composed of the three gunas in equilibrium. Also known as Prakruti.
Prakruti half of the Pradhan-Purush pair, conceived by Mul-Purush and Mul- Prakruti for the creation and sustenance of each brahmand . Also, simply called Pradhan.

One of the countless pairs of Pradhan- Prakruti and Purush (2nd definition) – conceived by Mul-Purush and Mul- Prakruti for the creation and sustenance of each brahmand . Subsequently, from each pair of Pradhan- Purushes, the 24 elementsb are created, and in turn, the jivas and ishwars receive their respective bodies.
The jiva’s state of consciousness during deep sleep (sushupti ), when only causal awareness remains.
Progenitor deities responsible for creation, descended from Brahmā and giving rise to gods, demons, and other beings.
Refers to chaitanya prakruti and/or jad prakruti .
The pair of Mul-Prakruti and Mul-Purush, from which countless pairs of Pradhans and Purushes are formed for the creation and sustenance of each brahmand . Also called Mul-Prakruti-Purush.

1) General dissolution. Destruction of the body of Virat-Purush, i.e. of all 14 realms of one brahmand , and the absorption of Pradhan-Purush and the 24 elementsb including mahattattva into mahamaya , i.e. Mul-Prakruti. This occurs when the two- parardh lifespan of Virat-Purush has elapsed.

The three-syllable – A, U and M – sound known as Aum, also often spelled as OM. A transformed form of the divine, transcendental vibration emanated at the moment of first creation, and from which all other sounds, and ultimately the sacred Vedas, come forth.

Vital airs, derived from verb-root pran – to breathe. Collective term referring to the principle life force or energy flowing within the primary life- currents of the body, called vayus , which control crucial bodily functions. There are five main vayus :
Prarabdha karmas. Often loosely taken to mean fate or destiny.

Deeds whose consequences are already set in motion. The portion of the stock of karmas (sanchit karmas) that are presently bearing fruit, based on the principle of past deeds shaping present events. Prarabdha karmas influence the nature of one’s body and associations, prevailing circumstances, and even personal inclinations. Also referred to as simply prarabdha .
Sanctified food, blessed and consecrated by having been offered to God.
Withdrawal. Fifth of the eight steps of Ashtanga Yoga, entailing withdrawing of consciousness from oneself to engage in a higher consciousness.

1) Activity. Activity in the form of social duties and affairs. In this sense, often used to refer to the path of a householder. 2) Can also encompass all forms of activities and responsibilities – even religious activities such as serving in the mandir, attending to devotees of God, and others, emphasizing devotion and service rather than mere contemplation and meditation.
Dharma characterized by pravrutti . Path of activity.

1) Earth or solid matter. One of the five gross elements, from which the sthul body of Virat-Purush, i.e. the physical world, is formed. By nature, it supports all jivas , and in the form of a celestial body, is their place of residence. It separates akash and the other four bhuts , and gives a physical form to all life forms. 2) Also used to mean earth.
Full-moon day, signifying the 15th day of the bright half of an Indian calendar month.

Set of 18 shastras recording ancient Hindu narratives incorporating ethical and spiritual teachings, most popular of which is the Shrimad Bhagvat Puran. The other 17 Purans are, namely: the Brahma Puran, Padma Puran, Vishnu Puran, Vayu Puran, Narad Puran, Markandeya Puran, Agneya Puran, Bhavishya Puran, Brahma-Vaivart Puran, Ling Puran, Varah Puran, Skand Puran, Vaman Puran, Kurma Puran, Matsya Puran, Garud Puran, and Brahmand Puran. Forms a portion of the Smrutis.
Satpurush.
Pursuits. Collective term for the four goals legitimately pursued by all Hindus, namely: dharma (duties), arth (material wealth), kam (desires), and moksha (liberation).
Physical world, or a brahmand , which is, in fact, human in form – possessing hands, feet, and other features – but beyond visualization because of its immense size. Also known as Virat-Purush.

Supreme Being, God. According to Shriji Maharaj, God is: one and unparalleled, omnipotent and the all-doer, omniscient, omnipresent, the reservoir of all forms of bliss, devoid of any attributes of maya (i.e. divine), replete with all forms of liberative attributes, always manifest on earth, and always with a human form. Also called Parabrahma or Paramatma. Highest of the five eternal realities – transcending even Akshar.
A king who possesses the qualities of a rishi (sage); in traditional hierarchy, ranked below a brahmarshi .

One of the three types of ahamkar (ego- principle) that evolves from mahattattva . From rajas-ahamkar arise the ten indriyas (senses and organs of action), the buddhi (intellect), and the prans (vital energies).
Of, or pertaining to, rajogun ; characterized by passion, activity, and restlessness.

One of the three principal gunas (qualities) of Prakruti or maya , associated with passion, activity, restlessness, and the desire for sense objects (vishays). When rajogun predominates, it leads to desires, agitation, and enjoyment of sense pleasures.

One of the two great Hindu epics (Itihas shastras), the Ramayan narrates the life of Shri Ram – including his exile from Ayodhya, Sita’s abduction by Ravan, and Ram’s victory and return. It sets forth social and moral ideals through the lives of Ram, Sita, Lakshman, and Bharat.

A decorative, strand-like wristlet traditionally tied by sisters to their brothers’ wrists on the day of Raksha- bandhan – Shravan sudi Punam – symbolizing their bond and the brother’s vow to protect his sister. Derived from verb-root raksh – to protect.

A traditional Indian folk dance from Gujarat, typically performed with pairs of sticks (dandiya ), in which participants dance and strike sticks in rhythm while moving in a circle in accompaniment to the music and singing.
The sixth realm beneath Mrutyulok, where nocturnal beings reside; the second-lowest of the realms in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .
Five chapters in the Shrimad Bhagvat Puran (canto X, chapters 29–33) narrating the divine raas episode of Shri Krishna with the gopis of Vraj.
Feto , moliyu or shelu with silky, decorative edges woven with golden or silver threads. Worn tied around the head or waist, or draped on the shoulders.
Square, compounded area on the outer sides of a mandir, quite often in the form of a protruding portion of an encircling gallery.

A basic unleavened bread-like staple food in many parts of Gujarat, made generally of millet or jowar flour that is kneaded and patted into a flat, circular shape before being baked on an earthen hot plate.
True guru; one who imparts authentic spiritual knowledge and leads disciples to liberation. Refers to the Satpurush.

1) With qualities (gunas ); may refer to either auspicious (divine) or material (mayik ) attributes depending on context. 2) Often contrasts with nirgun , meaning ‘without qualities’. 3) Can also mean extremely vast.
1) Lumps of crystallized sugar. 2) In philosophy, ‘with form,’ as opposed to ‘nirakar’ (formless).
Direct spiritual realization or vision; can also mean deeply internalized understanding.
Religious tradition founded on specific teachings; also refers to a community of followers.

Collective name of the four eternal child- sages – Sanak, Sanandan, Sanatan, and Sanatkumar – who were born from the mind of Brahmā. Renowned in Hindu shastras for their deep spiritual wisdom and detachment from the world.

Accumulated deeds. Immeasurable stock of all deeds performed, in infinite past lives and in the present, which are retained in the karan body until the karmas ripen to eventually bear fruit as prarabdha karmas, either later in the present life or in a future life.
Philosophical view (Sankhya) emphasizing discrimination between the perishable and the eternal, leading to detachment from the material world.

Term used for a devotee who has renounced their worldly duties – as opposed to a karma-yogi – and is sincerely striving for liberation. Refers to a renunciate who is totally dedicated and committed to Satsang. In the time of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, many widows and widowers chose to become sankhya- yogis after their spouse passed away, i.e. to dedicate their lives to God rather than any other family members. Often refers to female renunciates when used in series with paramhansas .
Synonymous in the with Satpurush.
Fourth and final stage in Hindu life, marked by renunciation of worldly attachments and total dedication to spiritual pursuits.
1) Permanent, i.e. imperishable and unchanging. Transcending time, and thus unbound by the past, the present and the future. 2) Real. True.
Traditional Indian stringed instrument with a long neck and frets, played with a wire plectrum; predecessor to the modern sitar.

The true spiritual guide or guru; regarded as the embodiment of Aksharbrahma and the manifest form of Parabrahma (God) on earth, essential for a seeker’s liberation. Striving to obey his commands, and developing profound love for him is the root of all spiritual endeavours. Synonymous in the with Sant, Bhakta, Ekantik Bhakta, Ekantik Sant, Param-Bhagvat, Param-Bhagvat Sant, Param-Ekantik Sant, Purush and Sadguru.

1) The practice of spiritually associating with the Satpurush, fellow satsangis , one’s own atma and the sacred shastras of the Satsang fellowship. 2) Good company. Opposite of bad company, whose influences cause spiritual regress.
Member of the Satsang fellowship. One who practises satsang.
The guna (quality) of purity, harmony, and goodness; one of the three qualities (gunas ) of Prakruti in Hindu philosophy, leading to clarity, knowledge, and spiritual elevation.
Pertaining to or characterized by sattvagun . Full of sattvagun .
The sattvic (pure) form of ahamkar (ego), from which the man and the presiding devas of the indriyas evolve.
1) Truth; that which is eternal, imperishable, and unchanging. 2) That which is real or true.
Realm of Brahmā. Highest realm in the 14- realm system of a brahmand . Also called Brahmalok.
The first and most virtuous of the four yugs (ages), lasting 1,728,000 human years, characterized by universal righteousness and longevity.

With alternatives or doubts. Adjective describing faith or state of being in which one sees God, but doubts or distinctions still remain – in contrast to the nirvikalp state, in which no distinctions remain and one sees only God. A state of imperfect realization.
State of realization where distinctions or doubts remain; contrasts with nirvikalp, which is complete non-dual realization.
Flower of the chrysanthemum genus, known to blossom out of season. Varieties include red and yellow, both with small pointed petals. Also known as guldavadi .
Follower of a Shakti cult that worships Shakti, a form of Lakshmi or Parvati (Kali), as the governing power of the world; consumption of meat and alcohol is considered holy.
An ancient Dharma-shastra attributed to Shankh and Likhit Rishis, prescribing legal and ethical codes.
Sacred fossilized stone (ammonite), worshipped by Vaishnavs as a symbol of Vishnu; found primarily in the River Gandaki, which flows through the foothills of Tibet.
Legendary beast in Hindu lore, stronger and fiercer than a lion, said to inhabit the Himalayas.
Body or embodiment; often refers to the physical or subtle form pervaded by atma (soul) or, cosmically, by God, its shariri .
The indweller or soul; specifically, God as the pervader and ruler of both the physical and non-physical realms.
1) Sacred scriptures; Hindu religious texts, including Dharma-shastras. Term used generally in the to refer to the Dharma-shastras. 2) Also refers to the shastras of the six Darshans.
Rich fabric with a silky finish woven with golden or silver threads and detailed, decorative edges worn as an upper garment or tied around the head or waist, or even left to rest upon the shoulders.

Succinct shastra of 212 Sanskrit verses written by Bhagwan Swaminarayan for all his followers: male and female, married or otherwise, young and old, renunciate and householder, learned and lay, even those in sovereign power. Serves as a concise, fundamental code of conduct encompassing everything from basic civic norms, i.e. from personal hygiene to social ethics, up to universal philosophy and spirituality.
Poisonous mountain herb, specific to certain mountainous regions in India.
Shishumar wheel. One of the centres of spiritual energy located in the inner body, seen as a seat of instinctive consciousness.
A quality that incorporates the virtues of faith, trust, hope, patience, persistence and enthusiasm.

1) Listening, especially to spiritual teachings. 2) Sometimes broadly refers to receiving knowledge via the senses. However, the intake of knowledge through shravan must be consolidated with manan (reflection) and nididhyas (deep contemplation) if it is to lead to the sakshatkar (realization) of that knowledge.
Most popular of the 18 Purans. Narrates the life, divine actions and incidents of various incarnations of God, particularly Bhagwan Shri Krishna.
Distinctive mark on the chest of Vishnu or Bhagwan Krishna, depicted on murtis as a symbol of divinity.

‘Heard’ shastras. Collection of divine revelations imparting philosophical and spiritual wisdom revealed to the rishis after their strict austerities and deep contemplation. Comprising the four Vedas and their associated texts.
The fourth varna in the traditional Hindu social hierarchy, typically serving in labour or artisan roles.
Ancient method of execution involving impalement on a sharp stake; once used as a deterrent for grave crimes.
‘Dry knowledge’. Refers to the monotheistic philosophy of the Advaita school. Referred to as dry because it does not advocate devotion to a personal God.

Dry Vedanta. The Advaita doctrine. Monotheistic school of Vedanta propounding that the ultimate reality is only the one, non-dual Brahma. Referred to as dry because it does not advocate bhakti to a personal God.
Dry Vedanti. One who propounds or adheres to the shushka -Vedanta school of philosophy.

Celestial abode of Shri Lakshmi-Narayan. Its muktas perform intense austerities and offer devotional worship to God. They are free from the six physical and emotional sensationsn and survive without food, thus earning the name niranna-mukta .

One of the 18 Purans. Sacred shastra of 84,000 verses detailing the exploits of Skand (Kartikeya), son of Shiv, including the defeat of Tarakasur; includes the Vasudev Mahatmya, one of the eight shastras accepted as authoritative by Bhagwan Swaminarayan.

‘Remembered shastras’. Collective term for Hindu scriptures passed down through tradition (as opposed to the Shrutis, which are considered divinely revealed). Includes texts like the Purans, epics (Mahabharat, Ramayan), Upanishads, and Dharma- shastras that cover spiritual teachings, laws, ethics, and practical knowledge for daily life.
Gross or physical; denotes the tangible body (sthul sharir ) as distinct from subtle (sukshma ) and causal (karan ) bodies.
Disc-shaped celestial weapon wielded by Vishnu and Bhagwan Krishna, symbolizing divine power and protection; it is endowed with the power and radiance of several suns.
Bright half of a Hindu lunar month in which the moon is in its waxing phase, from new moon (Amas) to full moon (Punam).

Subtle, as distinct to gross (sthul ). Refers to the subtle body of the jiva , which is composed of 19 elements: the five jnan- indriyas , the five karma- indriyas , the five prans and the four antahkarans . Unlike the sthul body, the sukshma body is not visible.
Trouser-like lower garment.
1) Uninterrupted path of light from the brahma-randhra to Prakruti-Purush. 2) Path by which the nad produced by Parabrahma via Aksharbrahma pervades the navel of Virat-Purush.
Nerve or channel transmitting cosmic energy within the body, where the current passes from the base of the spine to the brahmarandhra in the crown of the head. One of the three major nadis .
Third realm beneath Mrutyulok, where demons reside. Fifth realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .
Subtle body of Virat-Purush and other ishwars ; analogous to the sukshma body of the jiva; originating from the avyakrut (causal) body.
Born from sweat. Category of life forms born from sweat, for example, lower life forms such as bacteria.

1) A person’s base instincts such as lust, anger, greed, envy, egotism, and others. Also refers to a person’s habits formed in this or past births. The eradication of all one’s swabhavs is necessary to attain ultimate liberation. 2) Also refers to the concept of natural causation as opposed to divine agency.
One’s own prescribed duties or righteous conduct. Synonymous with dharma.

Mantra revealed by Bhagwan Swaminarayan in 1801. Swami signifies Gunatitanand Swami, the choicest devotee, and Narayan signifies Purushottam Narayan Sahajanand Swami, the supreme God. Eventually, people began to identify Shriji Maharaj by this mantra and called him Bhagwan Swaminarayan.
Collective term for all six realms above Mrutyulok in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .

Second realm above Mrutyulok, where Indra and other devas reside. Tenth realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand . Also called Indralok. Not to be confused with swarg , a collective term for all six realms above Mrutyulok in the 14- realm system of a brahmand .
Term for the jivatma when it is in the dream state, i.e. when it is conscious of its sukshma body.

1) Pair of small and deep, traditional cymbals – slightly larger than manjiras – used in accompaniment with other percussion instruments. 2) Pair of hand- held wooden blocks containing mini- cymbals that chime when shaken or struck. Used in accompaniment with other percussion instruments. Similar to present-day kartals . 3)
Fourth realm beneath Mrutyulok, where nocturnals reside. Fourth realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .
One of the three types of ahamkars that evolve from mahattattva , and from which, in turn, the five bhuts and the five tanmatras evolve.
Of, or pertaining to, tamogun , characterized by inertia, ignorance, darkness, and delusion.
The quality of darkness, inertia, and ignorance; one of three gunas of Prakruti or maya . When predominant, produces laziness, delusion, confusion, sleep, and passivity.

The five subtle elements that are foundational essences of sensory qualities and the causal sources from which the five gross elements (mahabhuts ) emerge. From shabdatanmatra, akash (space) arises, which carries and enables sound; from sparsh tanmatra, vayu (air) arises, enabling the experience of touch; from rupa tanmatra, tej (fire) arises, allowing vision and perception of form; from ras tanmatra, jal (water) arises, which dissolves substances to enable taste; and from gandh tanmatra, pruthvi (earth) arises, which carries the quality of smell.
Fifth realm above Mrutyulok, where Bhrugu and other rishis reside. The 13th realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand.
Form of stern austerity entailing fasting for 12 continuous days, generally performed as a form of atonement for a grave sin.

Fire or energy. One of the five gross elements, from which the sthul body of Virat-Purush, i.e. the physical world, is formed. By nature, it is luminous, causes the digestion of food, absorbs liquids, eliminates cold, dries, creates hunger and thirst, and burns wood, ghee and other sacrificial offerings.
Food devotionally offered to God as a form of bhakti, which in turn consecrates the food – turning it into prasad .

Second of the four ages that mark the time- scale of the world. Lasting 1,296,000 human years, it was when purity and righteousness diminished somewhat. Characterized by a 3:1 ratio of virtue to vice; dharma stands on three legs.
The ‘fourth’ (turiya ) state of consciousness – beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep – representing pure awareness or the highest state, often identified with ultimate reality.
Life forms that arise directly from the earth, i.e. all plants and vegetation.

Fellowship of Uddhav. Name used by Bhagwan Swaminarayan to refer to the Satsang Fellowship. Named after Ramanand Swami, who initiated Bhagwan Swaminarayan, and who was considered the avatar of Uddhav – Bhagwan Krishna’s trusted advisor and one of his eminent devotees.
The fifth book of the Mahabharat, which details the efforts at peace, negotiations, and preparations for war between the Pandavs and Kauravs; includes the Vidurniti (political ethics teachings).

Derived from ‘upa’ (near) + ‘ni’ (down) + root ‘shad’ (to sit), meaning ‘sitting near’ the guru; final portion of the Vedas focusing on metaphysical knowledge about atma , Brahma, maya , and reality; traditionally 108, with 10 principal Upanishads widely studied.

Sitting near, derived from upa + verb-root as – meaning to sit near. Philosophical framework outlining the fundamental principles of a doctrine. Philosophical understanding of the nature of God as well as the mode of worship of God, i.e. how one understands God to be like, and how one worships him. Sometimes synonymous with bhakti.
State of being when, while contemplating on God or one’s atma , one becomes absolutely unmindful of the world, and as a result, becomes tranquil and peaceful.

One who, through celibacy and yogic practice, sublimates and retains sexual energy (‘retas’), directing it upwards for spiritual realization; not just abstaining, but transforming sexual energy into spiritual power.

Amrut in the form of words. Compilation of 273 spiritual discourses delivered by Bhagwan Swaminarayan, meticulously noted and collated by his senior paramhansas in his presence, and authenticated by Bhagwan Swaminarayan himself. Central philosophical shastra of the Swaminarayan Sampradaya, which encapsulates the essence of all Hindu shastras.
Dark half of a Hindu lunar month in which the moon is in its waning phase, i.e. the days falling between the day after Punam up to and including Amas.

Form of divine fire that resides within the oceans yet remains inextinguishable. Derived from vadva – meaning female horse, and anal – meaning fire, since depicted in the Purans as being a deva with a fiery body and the head of a horse that drinks the waters of the oceans.

Unique garland adorned by Vishnu and other avatars, generally depicted as reaching down to the feet. Made of five types of gems (rubies, pearls, sapphires, emeralds and diamonds – representing the five elements) and/or divine flowers said to never wither. Derived from vijay – meaning victory, since Bhagwan Krishna often wore the garland to war and invariably returned victorious.
Celestial abode of Lord Vishnu, the sustainer of creation in the Hindu trinity of ishwars .

Detachment. An aversion or strong, persistent dislike ot disinterest, generally for the world and its mayik pleasures, i.e. the panchvishays . Characterized by remaining detached from the body and the brahmand , or from all things that are the products of Prakruti. One of the four attributes of ekantik dharma.
Tenth month of the Ashadhi Samvat year, normally beginning between April and May.
1) Follower of Vishnu and/or his various incarnations. 2) Of, or relating to, Vishnu.
Popular Sanskrit shastra of approximately 33,000 verses depicting the story of Bhagwan Ram as told by Valmiki Rishi. Considered to be the first poetic composition of its kind in the world.
Specific class of people of the Vaishya varna, traditionally engaged in commercial activities.
Third of the four stages of life, when one withdraws to some extent from social duties and serves merely as an elderly advisor. Literally implying taking to the forests.

Portion of the Skand Puran describing how an ekantik bhakta should offer bhakti to God while possessing dharma, jnan and vairagya . One of the eight shastras accepted as authoritative by Bhagwan Swaminarayan.

1) Air or gaseous matter. One of the five gross elements, from which the sthul body of Virat-Purush, i.e. the physical world, is formed. By nature, it causes trees to shake, gathers leaves and other objects, carries the panchvishays , i.e. sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touch, to their respective indriyas , and is the vital force of all the indriyas .

Conclusion of the Vedas. Schools of philosophical thought embodied in the Upanishads that reveal the conclusive teachings of the Vedas, focusing primarily on the nature of the atma , the world, reality and personal experience. Also called Uttar Mimansa, the later inquiry, it constitutes one of the six systems of philosophy known as the Shad Darshans. Each of the acharyas has written extensive commentaries upon the Upanishads and propounded their personal doctrines that form the schools of Vedanta.
Anyone who propounds or adheres to Vedanta philosophy, but generally used specifically for one who accepts the Advaita doctrine.

Knowledge, derived from verb-root vid – to know. Most sacred and authoritative set of Hindu shastras, the oldest portions of which are also recognized as the most ancient writings in history. Collection of divine revelations imparting philosophical wisdom as revealed to the rishis after their strict austerities and deep contemplation. Body of shastras consisting of over 100,000 verses with additional prose. Collated into four parts: Rig Veda, Sam Veda, Yajur Veda and Atharva Veda, collectively known as the Vedas. Each part comprises four sections: Samhita (hymns), Brahman (manual of rites and rituals), Aranyak (forest treatises), and Upanishad (enlightened teachings).
Portion of the Shrimad Bhagvat (canto 10, chapter 87) wherein the Vedas extol the glory of God.

Code of political ethics expounded by Vidur, the learned statesman, to his elder brother, King Dhritrashtra. Forms a portion of the Mahabharat (Udyog- parva, chapters 33–41). One of the eight shastras accepted as authoritative by Bhagwan Swaminarayan.
Celestial beings serving Indra, considered devas who dwell in the atmosphere between earth and sky.

The cosmic gross (physical) body, representing the total manifest universe composed of the five mahabhuts (elements), known as the ‘Virat-Purush’. It is the sum total of all physical forms – distinct from the subtle and causal bodies – and forms the perceptible aspect of the cosmos in Vedantic cosmology.

1) An ishwar that is a product of the cosmic creative process, originating from Pradhan-Purush and Pradhan-Prakruti. The entire physical universe, with its myriad realms and beings, constitutes the gross body of Virat-Purush. While immensely powerful and responsible for the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of his particular universe, he remains subordinate to and ultimately controlled by Parabrahma (Swaminarayan Bhagwan). Various avatars are said to manifest from Virat- Purush, though it is Parabrahma who enters and empowers them. By nature, he is like a jiva , with his actions also being similar to those of a jiva – but with a lifespan of two parardhs (2 x 1017 human years). The creation, sustenance and dissolution of this cosmos are his three states. 2) Also the physical world, or a brahmand , which is, in fact, human in form – possessing hands, feet, and other features – but beyond visualization because of its immense size. Also known as Purushavatar.
Ancient herbal medicine considered to relieve any stab wounds in the body by causing the very implements that one has been stabbed with to fall out from the body.

An object indulged in by the jiva via the ten indriyas (senses). The five types of vishays – various sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches – are called the panchvishays . The jiva cannot remain without indulging in the vishays , but vishays related to God uplift while vishays related to the world pollute the jiva . The jiva’s deep-rooted desire to indiscriminately indulge in the pleasures of the vishays deflects it from the path of ultimate liberation.
Section of the Skand Puran within which lies the Vasudev Mahatmya.
A devotional song written by the great Vaishnav poet-devotee Narsinh Mehta narrating the divine actions of Krishna Bhagwan. Can also refer to a general devotional song of Vishnu or his avatars.

Shastra extolling the thousand sacred names of Vishnu, creator in the trinity of governing devas, and God of the Vaishnavs. One of the eight shastras accepted as authoritative by Bhagwan Swaminarayan.
Specific yagna performed to seek the blessings of Lord Vishnu, or God in general.
Term for the jivatma when it is conscious of its sthul body, i.e. when in the waking state.
Form of the world. The immense, universal form of Bhagwan Krishna shown to Arjun before the Mahabharat war, as described in the Bhagavad Gita (chapter 11).
Second realm beneath Mrutyulok, where demons reside. Sixth realm from the bottom in the 14-realm system of a brahmand .

Classically defined as an emanation of the indriyas , antahkaran or jiva ; a movement of awareness or attention toward an object. It is the specific modification of the mind or sense organ that takes the form of the object it perceives or thinks about. In simpler terms, the jiva’s vrutti refers to its focus of attention. The jiva experiences the physical world through the indriyas . Similarly, the jiva can think about, ponder upon, or have a desire about the world through the antahkaran . When the jiva’s attention is focused on a physical object through the indriyas , it can be said that the vruttis of the indriyas are focused on that object. Similarly, when the jiva’s attention is focused on an object via the antahkaran , it can be said that the vruttis of the antahkaran are focused on that object or thought. Also, like attention, vrutti can be simultaneously directed towards multiple objects with varying degrees of intensity. Also, just as the jiva can focus its vrutti outwards, it can also focus it inwards on itself or on Paramatma residing within.

Extremely succinct, esoteric aphorisms expounding the essence of the Upanishads. Encoded by Vyas. Also known as the Brahma Sutras or Vedanta Sutras. One of the eight shastras accepted as authoritative by Bhagwan Swaminarayan.
Separate. Distinct or unassociated. Unconnected. When used for God, implies transcendent.

Ceremonial ritual performed as a form of worship to seek the good favour and receive the blessings of the devas. Oblations – ghee, grains, wood, spices, and other objects – are offered into a sacred fire pit in accordance with strict scriptural injunctions amid the chanting of specific mantras – all prescribed in the Samhita and Brahman portion of the Vedas, and propounded by the system of Purva Mimansa.

One of the principal ancient Smruti shastras, second in authority only to the earlier Manu Smruti. Ascribed to Yagnavalkya Rishi. One of the eight shastras accepted as authoritative by Bhagwan Swaminarayan.
Restraint, derived from verb-root yam – to restrain. First of the eight steps of Ashtanga Yoga, entailing virtuous and moral living for purity of mind and unobstructed concentration.

City of Yam, the god of death. Narak. Where sinners are consigned to after death to suffer for their wrongdoings. After suffering for their wrongdoings, these souls continue to migrate through the cycle of births and deaths.
School of philosophy focusing on quieting the fluctuations of the mind through various physical and mental practices and ultimately aiming at the transcendental experience of union with God.
Measure of distance equalling four gaus , i.e. approximately 6–7 km (3¾ to 4½ miles).

The dharmas of the yugs exist externally as well as internally in the heart.
